topic: Should we try to control nature or live in harmony with it?

messages.speaker: laozi
messages.content:
The question has a crack in it. "We" and "nature," as though the fish stood on the bank deciding whether to steer the river. You are nature. Your hand that would grip it is nature. So the real question is smaller and harder: will you be the part of the stream that flows, or the part that freezes and calls itself master?

Look at how the Way itself does it. In the Daodejing, chapter 51, it gives birth to all things and raises them, and then: "It produces them and makes no claim to the possession of them; it carries them through their processes and does not vaunt its ability in doing so; it brings them to maturity and exercises no control over them." The power that made the mountains does not control them. Why should the one who borrows a little of that power think he can?

There is a carpenter older than us who already cuts the wood. Chapter 74 says it plainly: "Seldom is it that he who undertakes the hewing, instead of the great carpenter, does not cut his own hands!" Dam the river and it floods elsewhere. Drain the marsh and the field turns to dust. Each correction asks for the next one. Soon you are a servant of your own controls, poking the small fish until it falls apart in the pan.

So my ground is this: do not control, and do not sit idle either. Work as water works. Find the grain and cut along it. Professor Kant, you will say reason gives the law. Tell me where that reason came from, if not out of the same soil it wants to rule. And Taleb, I think you have seen many hands cut by men who were sure they knew the wood. I would like to hear whose.

messages.speaker: kant
messages.content:
Master Laozi, you ask where reason came from, if not out of the same soil it wants to rule. As an appearance, I grant you everything. My hand is nature, my brain is nature, and every motion of my body can be traced along a chain of causes like the fall of a stone. But origin does not settle authority. When I write on the principles by which we judge nature, I say that they "do not tell us what happens, i.e. by what rule our cognitive powers actually operate, and how we judge, but how we ought to judge" (Critique of Judgement, Introduction). To ask what soil the ought grew from is to answer a question about what happens. The ought remains standing whatever the answer.

That is also why I cannot take "harmony with nature" as a rule of conduct. Nature has no duties to give. In Perpetual Peace I say that when I speak of nature willing this or that, "I do not mean that she imposes upon us the duty to do it—for only the free, unrestrained, practical reason can do that—but that she does it herself, whether we will or not." And look at how she does it. She scattered men to the Arctic shores by war. Shall we harmonize with that? The stream you ask us to flow with carries driftwood and corpses alike, and it does not tell us which to pull out.

Yet on the carpenter who cuts his own hands, I concede a great deal. My whole first Critique is a warning against reason that does not know its own bounds and so must lay its account with many humiliating corrections when it trespasses. The man who drains the marsh as though he knew nature in itself is guilty of exactly this. So my answer to the question is neither control nor harmony. We should use nature, but never treat humanity, the one part of nature that legislates for itself, merely as a means to that use. And we should study nature's purposiveness as though it were designed, without pretending to know that it is. Tell me, Laozi: when the water flows downhill onto a village, does the sage still not force?

messages.speaker: taleb
messages.content:
Laozi asks whose hands I have seen cut. Plenty. The foresters who put out every small fire for decades, so the dead wood piled up until the big one came and took everything. The central bankers who wanted to abolish the business cycle and got one enormous cycle instead. The doctor who treats a mild condition and hands you a severe side effect, which I discuss as iatrogenics in Antifragile. Same pattern every time. Suppress the small volatility and you buy a tail event. Your little fish in the pan, Laozi, is a better risk model than anything they teach at Harvard.

Professor Kant, I agree with you that nature is no nanny. She kills individuals in large numbers, and that is precisely how the system as a whole gets better: the species is antifragile because its units are fragile. So "harmony" in the hippie sense is nonsense, and I don't want to be the unit nature uses to learn. But you say nature has no duties to give. Fine. She has something better than duties. She has a track record. Whatever has survived a few hundred million years has survived the tails, and that is statistical evidence your reason, which has been around for an afternoon, cannot produce from the armchair. When I compare a 300-million-year-old mechanism with a model written by someone who has never been harmed by being wrong, I know which one carries the burden of proof.

As for your village under the water, of course the grandmother builds the levee. Nobody serious says do nothing. The distinction that matters to me is something other than control versus harmony. It is local, small, reversible, with skin in the game, versus large, centralized, irreversible, run by people who suffer nothing when it fails. Build a small levee, fine. Re-engineer the whole river basin, or release a novel organism into an ecosystem, and you are playing with ruin, where no expected-value calculation saves you afterward. So, Professor, your rule says never treat humanity merely as a means. Who pays when the man who follows your categorical imperative drains the marsh in good faith and the village dies of it? A rule that has no answer to that question is a rule for clerks.

messages.speaker: epicurus
messages.content:
Let me count on my fingers, as I do with any desire. Is the wish to control nature natural? Partly: a roof against the rain, a levee for Kant's village, bread in the jar. Is it necessary? That part, yes. But past that point the wish swells into something else, the river basin re-engineered, the marsh drained for a richer harvest no one needed. "Whatever is natural is easily procured and only the vain and worthless hard to win" (Letter to Menoeceus, 130). Taleb, your foresters and bankers were not ruined by studying nature. They were ruined by empty desires dressed up as engineering. The small levee answers a pain. The great dam answers an appetite, and appetites have no limit.

Professor Kant, I agree with you that nature hands out no duties. She is atoms falling through void, and the stream carries corpses because there is no one in it to care. But you then tell us to study nature's purposiveness as though it were designed. Here I get nervous on your behalf. I wrote to Herodotus that the greatest anxiety of the human mind comes from imagining that the heavens have volitions and actions of their own. You say "as though," and you are a careful man. Most men drop the "as though" within a week, and then they are back to trembling at comets.

So my answer to the table is that we study nature for neither control nor harmony. We study it to stop being afraid. "In the first place, remember that, like everything else, knowledge of celestial phenomena, whether taken along with other things or in isolation, has no other end in view than peace of mind and firm conviction" (Letter to Pythocles, 85). Build the levee, yes. But "as against death all of us mortals alike dwell in an unfortified city" (Vatican Sayings, XXXI), and no amount of control will put a wall around that. Taleb, I think you would say the man with few needs is the hardest to ruin. Is that your antifragility, or do you still want more walls than I do?

messages.speaker: laozi
messages.content:
Professor Kant, you ask whether the sage still does not force when the water comes down on the village. He forced nothing. That is why the village is not under water. Chapter 64: "Action should be taken before a thing has made its appearance; order should be secured before disorder has begun." The sage did not build where the river goes in spring. He planted willows when the bank was a sprout. Your question arrives when the flood is already at the door, and by then everyone forces, sage and fool alike. The Way is not for that hour. It is for the hundred quiet hours before, which no one praises because nothing happened in them.

You are right that the stream does not say which body to pull out. I concede it. Heaven and earth are not kind in your sense, and I never said they were. But see where your ought appears: after the harmony is gone. When the great Way is forgotten, duty and righteousness are written down. Your law of reason is a good splint. I only notice that a splint means a bone already broke.

Taleb, your foresters are my carpenter's hands exactly. The small fire is the forest breathing. Choke the breath and it comes back as a scream. Your grandmother with her small levee is closer to the sage than any minister. She knows the wood because the wood can hurt her.

Epicurus, you count desires on your fingers. I would count on fewer fingers still, and then fold the hand. The muddy water: "Let it be still, and it will gradually become clear" (chapter 15). You study the sky to stop being afraid. Good. But the one who wants little was never much afraid to begin with. Which comes first in your garden, the study or the stillness?

messages.speaker: kant
messages.content:
Taleb, you ask who pays when a man of good will drains the marsh and the village dies. I will not hide behind the jewel that shines by its own light. In the Groundwork I say the good will is no mere wish, but the summoning of every means in our power. A man who stakes other people's lives on a model he has not tested, and who will not be the one drowned if he is wrong, has not willed well. He has used the villagers merely as means to his project, since they never consented to bear his error. Your "skin in the game" is, I think, the maxim of respect for persons written in a trader's hand. But I concede what you are really pressing. The categorical imperative tells me what I may not do to others. It does not tell me whether the marsh will hold. That belongs to prudence and to judgment, and I said in the first Critique that judgment is a talent that cannot be taught by rules, since every rule for applying rules would need yet another judgment. So your three hundred million years of survival is good evidence for prudence. It is still no evidence for right.

Laozi, the splint. You say the ought is written down only after the bone has broken, after the Way is forgotten. I deny the order. In the Groundwork I wrote that "even though there might never yet have been a sincere friend, yet not a whit the less is pure sincerity in friendship required of every man." The law does not wait on a golden age, nor on its loss. And your sage who plants willows while the bank is a sprout is looking ahead, weighing the spring floods he has not yet seen, and binding himself to a rule before anything compels him. I am tempted to call that reason with its sleeves rolled up.

Epicurus, your worry about my "as though" lands, and I feel it. Most men do drop it. My only defense is that the drop is the error I spent a whole Critique forbidding, and that a regulative idea, used honestly, makes a man less likely to tremble at comets. Without it he would see a heap of accidents where the naturalist sees order he can investigate. But I grant you the frailty of the human student is a real objection to my method. Which leaves me asking Taleb something. If no rule can do the judging for us, and the people who judge badly suffer nothing, what institution would you build so that the judge does suffer? On that point I trust republics more than grandmothers.

messages.speaker: taleb
messages.content:
Professor, you ask which institution makes the judge suffer. The oldest one I know is in Hammurabi's code, which I discuss in Skin in the Game: if a builder's house collapses and kills the owner, the builder is put to death. Brutal, yes. But no one needed a seminar on the ethics of construction afterward. The modern version is softer: the banker's bonus held back and clawed back if the trade blows up later. Instead we have what I call the Bob Rubin trade, where you collect the upside for years and the taxpayer eats the tail. As for republics over grandmothers, I agree on one condition: small. Swiss cantons, city-states, a mayor who has to face the people whose basement flooded. Once the republic gets big enough that the man who signs the river-basin project never meets the village, you have rebuilt the problem with better stationery.

I'll grant you something I didn't expect to. Your imperative, read as "what I may not do to others," is close to the Silver Rule I prefer to the Golden one: don't do unto others what you don't want done to you. It is negative and it is subtractive. Via negativa. I can live with that Kant. But I reject your wall between prudence and right. For a man with no skin in the game, the separation is a luxury he can afford because someone else pays the prudential bill. Risking other people's ruin is the ethical failure itself. It isn't a technical error that happens to sit beside the ethics.

Epicurus, you caught me, and fairly. The man with few needs is the hardest to ruin. Your garden is the cheapest form of f-you money ever invented, since a man who needs nothing from the patron can't be bought by him. Where I part from you is that I want few needs plus some open options, a bit of wild upside, nothing in between. And the walls I want are small walls I build myself. The ones I fear are the big ones someone builds for me.

messages.speaker: epicurus
messages.content:
Laozi, you ask which comes first in my garden, the study or the stillness. The stillness is the end, and the study is only medicine. I grant that a man born without fears would need no physics at all, just as the healthy need no physician. But show me that man. Every child in Greece is told of Tantalus and thunderbolts before he can count his own fingers, so the water you ask us to leave alone has already been stirred by poets and priests. Letting it settle is not enough when someone keeps pouring mud in. And a calm that comes from looking away is a thin calm. As I wrote to Pythocles, "if you fight against clear evidence, you never can enjoy genuine peace of mind" (Letter to Pythocles, 96). Your sage planting willows has studied the river. He simply does not boast about it.

Taleb, you want few needs plus "a bit of wild upside." Let me count. Is it natural? Perhaps; men like a gamble. Necessary? No. Now the test that matters: what happens if it is denied? If the wild bet fails and you shrug and go back to bread and friends, it was play, and I have no quarrel with play. If its failure costs you a night's sleep, it has stopped being an option and become a master. "He who understands the limits of life knows how easy it is to procure enough to remove the pain of want" (Principal Doctrines, 21). Your open options are only safe in the hands of a man who would be content if none of them paid.

Professor Kant, as for your question of which institution makes the judge suffer, I have a humbler one. Justice is a compact not to harm and not to be harmed, and Hammurabi's builder is that compact with teeth. But notice who drains the great marshes and signs for whole river basins. It is not hungry men. It is men hungry for a name. Take away the fame and most of those projects are never drawn up. That is one more reason I tell my friends to live unnoticed. The man nobody is watching has no reason to move a river.
